physics-h3-q2.s.s1.prompt: A charged particle of mass m and charge q enters perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B at speed v and undergoes uniform circular motion. Which option correctly gives the radius r and period T of its circular orbit?
physics-h3-q2.s.s1.explain: From the centripetal force equation, $\frac{mv^2}{r} = qvB \implies r = \frac{mv}{qB}$. The period is $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$, and, remarkably, this cyclotron period is independent of the orbit radius and speed.
physics-h3-q2.s.s2.prompt: Which scenario demonstrates the correct real-world application of this principle?
physics-h3-q2.s.s2.explain: The fundamental principles of this inquiry are widely implemented in modern technology.

physics-killer-12.material: Two parallel conducting rails a distance $\ell=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ apart lie on a horizontal surface, joined at one end through a resistor. The closed circuit formed by the rails, the conducting rod and the resistor has a total resistance of $2\,\Omega$. A uniform vertical magnetic field $B=0.5\,\mathrm{T}$ covers the whole circuit, and the rod moves along the rails at a constant speed of $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ away from the resistor. While the rod moves $2\,\mathrm{m}$ in $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, the magnetic flux through the circuit changes by $\Delta\Phi=B\ell\Delta x$. Which option correctly gives, in order, the magnitude of the induced current in the circuit and the magnitude of the external force needed to keep the rod at constant speed? (There is no friction.)
physics-killer-12.thinking.0: The Photoelectric Effect, the Duality of Light, and the Microscopic World
physics-killer-12.s.s1.prompt: Two parallel conducting rails a distance $\ell=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ apart lie on a horizontal surface, joined at one end through a resistor. The closed circuit formed by the rails, the conducting rod and the resistor has a total resistance of $2\,\Omega$. A uniform vertical magnetic field $B=0.5\,\mathrm{T}$ covers the whole circuit, and the rod moves along the rails at a constant speed of $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ away from the resistor. While the rod moves $2\,\mathrm{m}$ in $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, the magnetic flux through the circuit changes by $\Delta\Phi=B\ell\Delta x$. Which option correctly gives, in order, the magnitude of the induced current in the circuit and the magnitude of the external force needed to keep the rod at constant speed? (There is no friction.)
physics-killer-12.s.s1.explain: $\Delta\Phi=B\ell\Delta x=0.5\cdot0.5\cdot2=0.5\,\mathrm{Wb}$, $|\mathcal E|=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{0.5}{0.5}=1.0\,\mathrm{V}$ (agrees with $B\ell v=0.5\cdot0.5\cdot4$). $I=\dfrac{\mathcal E}{R}=\dfrac{1.0}{2}=0.5\,\mathrm{A}$. The magnetic force on the rod is $F=BI\ell=0.5\cdot0.5\cdot0.5=0.125\,\mathrm{N}$ (opposing the motion, by Lenz's law), so the external force is also $0.125\,\mathrm{N}$. Check: power $Fv=0.125\cdot4=0.5\,\mathrm{W}=I^2R=0.25\cdot2$. Omitting $\ell$ gives $I=1.0\,\mathrm{A}$ (option 1); omitting $\ell$ in the force gives $0.25\,\mathrm{N}$ (option 2); multiplying $\mathcal E$ by $\frac12$ gives option 4.
physics-killer-12.s.s2.prompt: Which scenario demonstrates the correct real-world application of this principle?
physics-killer-12.s.s2.explain: The fundamental principles of this inquiry are widely implemented in modern technology.
physics-killer-12.s.s1.hint.0: Faraday's law $|\mathcal E|=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=B\ell v$, $I=\dfrac{\mathcal E}{R}$. At constant speed the external force equals the magnetic force $F=BI\ell$.
